Massah and Meribah
MAS-uh MER-ih-buh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Massah, "testing," and Meribah, "strife"; the place at Rephidim where Israel tempted the LORD and Moses struck the rock.

📖 Biblical Definition

Massah ("testing") and Meribah ("strife") were the twin names given to the place at Rephidim where Israel, lacking water, quarreled with Moses and put the LORD to the test. "And he called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?" (Exo 17:7). At the LORD's command Moses struck the rock in Horeb, and water came out for the people to drink (Exo 17:6). The sin was grievous: having seen the plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, and the cloud, Israel still doubted God's presence and demanded proof. Scripture treats Massah and Meribah as a lasting warning against unbelief and the testing of God: "Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness: when your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my work" (Psa 95:8-9), a text the Epistle to the Hebrews applies to the church (Heb 3:8). Massah and Meribah stand in the dictionary as the place of Israel's provocation, a solemn warning that to doubt God's presence and goodness after all His proven mercies is to harden the heart and tempt the LORD, and a call to believe and trust Him in the dry places rather than to chide and test Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The place at Rephidim ("testing" and "strife") where Israel, lacking water, tempted the LORD asking "Is the LORD among us, or not?" (Exo 17:7); a lasting warning against unbelief and hardening the heart (Psa 95:8; Heb 3:8).

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Massah and Meribah need no defense from redefinition; their lesson is the sin of tempting God and hardening the heart in unbelief despite His proven mercies.

expand to see more

Unbelief-excused correction. The natural heart, meeting hardship, doubts God's presence and demands fresh proof, as Israel did asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?" Scripture names this tempting of God a grievous sin, committed by a people who had already seen His mighty works. The dictionary holds that to distrust God's goodness and presence after all His proven mercies is unbelief, not honest doubt; the believer is called to trust the God who has shown Himself faithful, even in the dry places where no water yet appears.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning against hardening the heart. The Holy Spirit, through the Psalm and the Epistle to the Hebrews, holds up Massah and Meribah to the church: "Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation" (Heb 3:8). The dictionary commends this solemn application: persistent unbelief hardens the heart and provokes the LORD, and the people of God in every age must hear His voice today, believe His promises, and not repeat the provocation of the wilderness.
